idiom_name: import-time initialisation (module body) or application factory + asyncio eager task factory
implementation_notes: Python's eager-acquisition idiom is execution at import: a module body runs exactly once, at first import, so building the client, pool or index there - or in an application factory/lifespan hook - guarantees consumers see a ready object. Modern asyncio adds an explicit switch: asyncio.eager_task_factory() makes a coroutine begin executing synchronously during Task construction instead of being scheduled, which the documentation presents as a performance improvement because the loop-scheduling overhead disappears for tasks that never block. Pools add pre-sizing and validation at open time. Prefer the explicit factory/lifespan path for long-lived processes and keep import-time construction for genuinely static, cheap-to-build singletons.
pitfalls: Import-time acquisition hides latency at first import and can deadlock: two modules that import each other and perform I/O in their bodies end up observing partially initialised modules.

In preforking servers (gunicorn --preload, multiprocessing fork) eagerly opened sockets, pools and threads are inherited by the children - a classic duplicated-fd and broken-connection bug; acquire after the fork.
A failure during import leaves the module absent from sys.modules, so 'retry' means re-importing and every consumer must cope with the transient absence.
